Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPA Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Nord Stream bombings were not us, Zelenskyy insists After two arrests, Ukraine’s president says Germany ‘well aware’ Kyiv was not involved in planning or execution of sabotage mission. What we know on day 1,643 Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Sun 23 Aug 2026 21.13 EDT Last modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 23.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Volodymyr Zelenskyy has insisted the Ukrainian government did not take part in the 2022 bombing of the Nord Stream undersea gas pipelines . Ukraine’s president said Germany was “well aware that Ukraine did not stand behind the execution or the very conception of this operation”. On Wednesday a Ukrainian man was arrested in Croatia on suspicion of taking part in the bombings. He was reportedly working on a film about the plot when arrested. German prosecutors allege he collaborated with another Ukrainian man who was arrested in Italy in 2025. German prosecutors allege the Nord Stream bombings were ordered by the Ukrainian state . Zelenskky has always denied his country’s involvement. He said Kyiv was helping Berlin with its investigation and hoped it would not cause a rift in relations. “It is very important for us not to lose our partnership, not to lose the trust of European countries that have been helping Ukraine since the very beginning of this war.” The pipelines were built to carry natural gas from Russia to Germany. The “coalition of the willing” supporting Ukraine will meet in Kyiv of Monday . The meeting will be jointly chaired by the leaders of Britain, France and Germany. Ukraine on Monday celebrates independence while also marking exactly four and a half years since the Russian full-scale invasion of 24 February 2022. Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister, is set to announce that the British government will let defence firm MBDA release classified information so Ukraine and France can set up local production of the long-range Storm Shadow/Scalp missile, writes Kiran Stacey and Dan Sabbagh . Emmanuel Macron, the French president, has pledged Paris will deliver new the SAMP/T interceptor system, said to be capable of shooting down some types of ballistic missiles. The Russian ⁠online retailer Ozon ⁠said a drone attack caused a ​major fire ⁠that shut down its ⁠logistics ​hub ‌in ‌Krasnodar in southern ‌Russia . Ukraine also hit Ozon warehouses in the central Orenburg region on Sunday, and the day before that, in the neighbouring Samara region . “After Ukrainian units hit the 15 largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it is now Ozon’s turn,” said a Ukrainian defence ministry announcement. Authorities in Krasnodar claimed two ⁠children were killed and ⁠another ⁠nine people were ⁠injured when drone debris hit ⁠a private ​childcare ‌centre. There was no independent confirmation. Early on Sunday, a drone attack was under way against an industrial area ⁠of Nevinnomyssk ‌in ‌Russia’s southern Stavropol ‌region , its governor said. Nevinnomyssk is ⁠a major ​chemical production ​area. A ⁠Russian attack on the ⁠outskirts ⁠of Kharkiv in ​Ukraine’s north-east killed ⁠three people , the regional governor ⁠said ​late on Sunday. Emergency services evacuated ‌eight people, some of whom ​were injured, said Oleh Syniehubov, ⁠adding that a search was under way for ​other ‌possible ​casualties. Zelenskyy has said holding elections in Ukraine during wartime could split the country. Dan Sabbagh writes that Zelenskyy was responding to a demand for elections by Mykhailo Fedorov whom he sacked as defence minister. Supporters have distanced themselves from Fedorovo because of his call for elections . Zelenskyy said on Saturday: “I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then during such a war we can move in the selection of elections … Elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine.” Elections have been suspended by law in Ukraine since martial law was imposed in response to the Russian invasion . Zelenskyy said on Saturday that if Ukraine’s allies established “specific conditions” for a safe, legitimate and democratic election process he would support it. It would require “the participation of the military, in frontline territories, abroad, where millions of our citizens have gone, fleeing the war” and would have to occur “without strikes and shelling”. Zelenskyy said he had removed Fedorov as defence minister because he had overreached , intruding on functions belonging to the military. He was offered four alternative jobs in the government but declined them. “I really had and still have a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo,” Zelenskyy said. “We have been through a lot together. But I believe that he himself goes, or is pushed, into the wrong things.” Ukraine thinks that Russian president Vladimir Putin is planning to draft an additional 300,000 troops for the war after Russian parliamentary elections ⁠in mid-September. Zelenskyy described a “peripheral mobilisation” targeting Russia’s far-flung regions. “We ⁠believe it will not take place in the central cities,” he said. “But I don’t think they will be able to hide ​it very well.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Russia Europe explainers Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Beállítom A Bajnokok Ligája idei szezonját szerdán elkezdte a Liverpool is, az Atlético Madrid volt az ellenfelük az első fordulóban. Tavaly is a spanyolokkal szemben kezdték meg az alapszakaszt, és egy éve hazai pályán 3-2-re győztek. Szoboszlai Dominik már az első másodpercekben felgyorsított egy labdaszerzés után, a sprintje végén jó helyzetbe hozta Isakot, de a csatár mellélőtt. A 17. percben vezetést szereztek a spanyolok, Llorente kapott nagyszerű indítást Julián Álvareztől, Kerkez Milos nem helyezkedett a legjobban, a csatár megigazította a labdát mellette, és 17 méterről a kapuba emelte. Alissonnak nem sokkal később nagyot kellett védenie, hogy megakadályozza a kétgólos hátrányt, akkor Álvarez távolról szúrta rá. A 40. percben egyenlített a Liverpool. Kerkez szerzett labdát az ellenfél térfelének közepén, Isakhoz passzolt, akinek a lövése kijött a kapusról. A kipattanóra Szoboszlai csapott le, de elsőre nem talált lövőhelyzetet, de amikor az előre húzódó Araujo sarokkal vissza tudta elé tenni a labdát, akkor tíz méterről higgadtan és okosan gurította el a labdát a jobb alsóba. A Liverpool új szerzeményének, Barcolának, és a tavalyi sztárigazolásnak, Wirtznek is volt helyzete az első félidőben, de a kapu előtt nem voltak olyan határozottak, mint a magyar középpályás. Az 50. percben már előnybe került a Liverpool. Egy kipattanó labdára az argentin Mac Allister érkezett, és 18 méterről ballal, tökéletesen lőtt, mintaszerűen szorította le a lábfejét, és jól is helyezte a labdát, ami olyan erővel ment, hogy a vetődő Oblak kapus nem tudott védeni. A folytatásban is nagy tempót láttunk, de gólt már nem. Szoboszlait a meccs emberének választották. Sallai Roland is kezdő volt a Galatasaray-ban – a jobbhátvéd pozíciójában számítottak rá ezúttal is –, és a török bajnokcsapat már az ötödik percben vezetést szerzett egy öngóllal a Sporting otthonában. A portugálok Catamo góljával egyenlítettek, Suarez pontos büntetője pedig már a fordítást jelentette, Zalazar zárta le a meccset. A címvédő PSG kellemes ellenfelet, a Slovant kapta a bemutatkozó meccsén, és Dembélé gyors duplája után Ferran Torres triplázott, az 57. percben már 5-0-ra vezetett a francia csapat. A szlovákok erejéből a szépítésre futotta, a végeredményt Fabian Ruiz alakította ki. A Napoli és Arsenal nagy csatát vívott egymással, mindkét oldalon sok helyzet maradt ki, az egyetlen gólt a norvég Ødegaard érte el, a 75. percben szép háromszögelés után 18 méterről a kapufa segítsgével lőtt a kapuba. Az olaszoknak erre nem volt válaszuk. A Barcelona a 18:45-kor kezdődő meccsen folytatta a bajokságban megkezdett sorozatát, és a BL-ben is öt gólig jutott, a holland Feyenoord nem tudta megnehezíteni a katalánok dolgát. A Barca öt meccset játszott eddig idén, és már negyedik alkalommal talált ötször a kapuba. Raphinha duplázott – már a harmadik percben eredményes volt –, Lamine Yamalé volt a negyedik gól, az 5-1-es végeredményt a nyáron igazolt brazil center, Gabriel Jesus állította be. A másik délutáni meccsen a Stuttgart 3-1-re verte a norvég bajnok Stavangert. Finland, Sweden and Norway modernise underground infrastructure as Russia’s war in Ukraine revives fears of conflict on their soil By Rafael Yaghobzadeh Mon 21 Sep 2026 07.00 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Across Finland , Sweden and Norway, cold war bunkers are being given a new lease of life as Russia’s war in Ukraine revives fears of conflict in northern Europe. In the three countries, the work brings together multiple eras. The traces of the second world war and the cold war now coexist with contemporary infrastructures, revealing how these societies have adapted their protective measures over the decades. View image in fullscreen The underground levels of a hotel in Helsinki. Finland has about 50,500 civil defence shelters with space for a total of 4.8 million people – a substantial proportion of its almost 5.7 million population. Most (approximately 85%) are private, reinforced concrete shelters in individual buildings. In Helsinki, the entrance to one of the city’s largest shelters is hidden behind an ordinary car park. Thirty metres underground, a tunnel designed to absorb the blast of an explosion leads to a vast complex protected by two 13-tonne steel doors and a decontamination chamber. The bunker contains football and hockey pitches, a gym, a children’s playground, a cafe and even an area with inflatable structures. View image in fullscreen Formula Center, a go-kart track located in a bunker in Helsinki. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen A Swedish tourist plays a game of axe-throwing in a bunker, and a reservist trains at a shooting range set up in a bunker, in Helsinki. This is the paradox at the heart of Finland ’s civil-defence system: spaces designed for war have become part of everyday life. Across Helsinki, underground bunkers now contain a 300-metre karting track, a popular axe-throwing club, garages and a shooting range used by reservists. Another complex, completed in 1993, can shelter up to 3,800 people but normally operates as a swimming pool, complete with an Olympic-sized basin, water slides, diving boards, a gym and a sauna. View image in fullscreen A children’s playground set up inside the Merihaka bunker in Helsinki. View image in fullscreen A sport room set up in the Hakaniemi bunker in Helsinki. Behind these recreational spaces, however, the original infrastructure remains intact. Ventilation systems, filters, emergency beds, showers and facilities for dry toilets are regularly maintained. One of Helsinki’s public shelters can accommodate 6,000 people, and the city has 15 other large shelters of the same type. Private companies are allowed to use some of them during peacetime, provided they can clear the premises within 72 hours if the authorities issue an alert. View image in fullscreen The entrance to a recently renovated bunker, exceptionally open to the public, in Helsinki. View image in fullscreen The entrance to a bunker in a working-class neighbourhood in Helsinki. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen The Itäkeskus aquatic and multi-sports centre installed in a bunker, in Helsinki. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen The entrance to a bunker in Helsinki. A mother and her child emerge from the Merihaka bunker in Helsinki. View image in fullscreen Kamppi metro station in Helsinki would also serve as a nuclear shelter. Combined with mandatory shelters in the basements of residential buildings, Helsinki’s capacity exceeds the city’s population of almost 700,000. For decades, this system was regarded by many as a costly legacy of the cold war. Now the mood has changed. View image in fullscreen Jukka Lehtiranta, head of the Civil Defence Association in Helsinki. “It was a debate before, but thanks to Putin, it no longer is,” says Jukka Lehtiranta, the head of Helsinki’s Civil Defence Association. He continues to train volunteers for a possible wartime emergency. The oldest bunker he shows visitors dates from 1941. During the second world war, 38 families took refuge there from Soviet bombing. Today, the bunker remains fully operational. View image in fullscreen A bunker in Stockholm has become the home of a Bahnhof datacentre. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen An employee at work, and reflections at the Bahnhof data centre. View image in fullscreen The entrance to the Katarinaberget bunker – one of the largest in Europe – in Stockholm, Sweden. In Sweden , some of these cold war spaces have found a very different purpose. Thirty metres beneath Stockholm, a former bunker houses the datacentre of the Swedish company Bahnhof. Generators stand beside a wall of vegetation, while rows of computer servers occupy a vast chamber carved into granite and gneiss. The company sees the underground facility as more than a striking piece of architecture. Meanwhile, the country takes the risk of conflict very seriously. Conscription, which had been suspended in 2010, was reinstated in 2017. Norway reveals another layer of this history. In Bodø, a bunker built during the German occupation was part of the Atlantic Wall. Restored in 2014, it is now a museum maintained by former air force personnel. Its thick concrete walls still contain an air-filtration system, communications equipment and an Enigma machine once used by the German military. View image in fullscreen A second world war bunker near a building under construction in Bodø, Norway . View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen But Norway also illustrates what happens when civil defence infrastructure is allowed to deteriorate. The country has about 18,600 shelters, yet stopped building new ones after 1998. Oslo’s largest shelter, designed for 1,100 people, has not been renovated since 1992. Following Finland and Sweden , Norway has shifted to “total defence” mode this year The concept is designed to prepare all sectors of society, including the armed forces, government agencies, and businesses, for a major crisis or even war. View image in fullscreen Members of the Norwegian civil defence service emerge from a bunker beneath a school in the suburbs of Oslo, Norway. Across the three countries, these places reveal the uneasy coexistence of ordinary life and preparation for war. Bunkers have become swimming pools, sports centres, museums and datacentres, while their doors, filters and ventilation systems remain ready for a crisis. The war in Ukraine has given these hidden spaces a new significance. What once seemed like relics of a vanished conflict are once again being considered essential infrastructure.
